headline: New moon springs push bay stripers to the bridges as fluke bail out to the channels
subhead: Warm shallows in Greenwich Bay and the Providence River are shoving the doormats toward deeper water, while the new moon sets up the best sunset tide of the month.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July — it got soft and warm on top and started sorting fish by depth. We had a stretch of light, shifting wind out of the southwest most afternoons, which is enough to push a chop across Greenwich Bay and the upper river but not enough to mix the water down. That's the setup that bakes the shallows. Fluke that were spread across the flats off Warwick Neck and up into Greenwich Bay in June have been sliding out toward the channel edges and the mouths of the coves, looking for the cooler water stacked against the bottom structure. Stripers, meanwhile, have been doing their usual summer thing — daytime fish going quiet and deep around the bridge pilings, night fish waking up hard on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming.

This week the moon's the story. We're coming off new moon, which means spring tides — bigger swings, more current, more water moving through the East and West Passages than we've seen in a couple weeks. That extra push does two things: it flushes bait out of the coves and rivers on the outgoing, and it stacks that bait against structure on the incoming. The sunset-to-dusk window lines up with the top of the flood the next few nights, which is the alignment I wait for all summer — bass feeding right as the light goes, right as the current's still got some shove left in it. If you've only got one evening this week, Friday through Monday is when I'd take it, before the tides start easing off the neap side again.

Fluke fishing has been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight about it — the upper bay bite has cooled off as the water's crept up into the high 70s in the shallows. Greenwich Bay and the flats off Nayatt have gone soft during the day. The fish didn't disappear, they moved. Guys working the drop-offs along the Prudence Island channel edge, and down around Popasquash Point where the current runs harder, have been picking at keepers in 18 to 25 feet on the outgoing tide — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's really moving. It's not a banner bite. You're working for three or four keepers over a tide instead of a dozen, but the fish that are coming over the rail have been decent, a few pushing 4 and 5 pounds. If the water keeps climbing, expect more of that shift toward the bay mouth and the East Passage over the next couple weeks.

Stripers are the better story right now. The bridges — Mount Hope, the Jamestown-Newport span — have been holding fish tight to the pilings after dark, and with these spring tides pushing more current through, the bait's getting pinned right where the bass want it. Live eels drifted on the down-current side of the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing have been money, and swimming a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig off the rocks at Rocky Point and Nyatt Point has been picking up fish in the 26 to 34 inch range right at first light and again at dusk. Conimicut Point is still worth a pass on the outgoing — the flat there dumps bait right off the edge, and I've seen schoolie-to-mid-30s action for guys throwing white bucktails and swimming plugs along that drop. Nothing's blitzing. This is a tide-and-timing bite, not a run-and-gun bite. Fish the moving water around the structure and you've got a shot; fish the slack and you're just casting.

Scup have been consistent, which is the one thing you can count on in July. The ledges off Rocky Point, the rock piles around Prudence Island, and the Nyatt Point drop are holding good numbers on squid strips and clam bellies fished on top-and-bottom rigs, mostly in 15 to 30 feet. Nothing huge, but steady action, and a good way to fill a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn for bass. Black sea bass have shown up around the rockier structure near Jamestown and the Prudence Island shoreline — smaller fish mostly, a few keepers mixed in on squid and Gulp on jigheads worked slow along the bottom.

Bluefish have started trickling in — snapper blues in the coves and up in the Providence River, which tells me the bigger cocktail blues aren't far behind if the pattern holds like it usually does in late July. Weakfish, on the other hand, are still a no-show. The water's been warm enough for a while now, and that used to be the trigger, but it hasn't produced a single report I trust. I'm not chasing them until I see actual fish, not just the right temperature on a app.

Looking ahead: if the spring tides keep pushing current through the passages the way they have been, I'd fish the bridge pilings and the rocky points on the sunset flood through Monday — that's the best alignment we've had since before the full moon in June. After that the tides ease toward neap, current slows, and I'd expect the bass to spread out and get lazier, which usually means switching from moving structure to holding areas — deeper holes off Prudence and the channel bends where fish can sit out of the current and still eat. Plan B if the bass go quiet: keep working the fluke on the channel edges, because that fish isn't leaving the bay, it's just leaving the shallows.
